lesson.title: The Trap Lesson
lesson.subtitle: depuis + present tense: why ongoing actions stay in the present in French.

hook.title: Defusing the #1 English Transfer Trap: Present + depuis
hook.content: Whenever an English sentence says 'I have lived here for...', 'I have been learning French for...', or 'She has been waiting since...', ask: Is it still going on right now? Yes! So French keeps the verb in the PRESENT tense + depuis!

footnotes.title: Why 'for three years' in an ongoing sentence is depuis trois ans
footnotes.content: Whether English says 'since Monday' (depuis lundi) or 'for three years' (depuis trois ans), French uses depuis with the present tense!

pattern.title: Still Happening Now = Present Tense + depuis
pattern.content: Convert English 'have been [verb]-ing for/since X' directly into French Present Tense + depuis X.
pattern.linguist_note: French depuis marks the left boundary of a state extending through utterance time.
pattern.trap_note: Never translate 'for three years' with *pour trois ans in an ongoing duration sentence — use depuis trois ans!

exercises.prompt: Match each English ongoing-duration sentence with its French Present + depuis equivalent:

matching_pairs.english: I have been living here for five years
I have been learning French for a year
matching_pairs.german: J'apprends le français depuis un an

matching_pairs.english: We have been waiting for twenty minutes
She has been here since Monday

exercises.target_answer: J'habite ici depuis cinq ans, J'apprends le français depuis un an, Nous attendons depuis vingt minutes, Elle est ici depuis lundi
exercises.meaning: I have been living here for five years, I have been learning French for a year, We have been waiting for twenty minutes, She has been here since Monday
exercises.explanation: Every ongoing action uses the French present tense + depuis.

exercises.prompt: Translate 'I have known your brother for ten years' (and still know him!):
options: J'ai connu ton frère depuis dix ans
Je connais ton frère depuis dix ans
Je connais ton frère pour dix ans
exercises.target_answer: Je connais ton frère depuis dix ans
exercises.meaning: Present tense Je connais + depuis dix ans
exercises.explanation: Because you still know him today, use present tense Je connais + depuis!

exercises.prompt: What is the literal structure of 'Elle attend le bus depuis dix minutes'?
exercises.german: Elle attend le bus depuis dix minutes
exercises.natural: She has been waiting for the bus for ten minutes
options: She waited the bus during ten minutes
She has been waiting for the bus for ten minutes
She waits-for the bus since ten minutes
exercises.target_answer: She waits-for the bus since ten minutes
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: She waits-for the bus since ten minutes

exercises.prompt: Fold the direct object noun phrase into its pre-verbal clitic pronoun:
exercises.shift_hint: le / la / les before the verb
exercises.full_sentence: Je vois le train et je prends le train
exercises.explanation: Unlike English, French pulls the object pronoun le directly in front of the conjugated verb: Je le prends.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: Mon frère travaille ici depuis janvier
exercises.target_answer: Mon frère travaille ici depuis janvier
exercises.meaning: My brother has been working here since January
exercises.explanation: depuis covers both 'for [a span]' and 'since [a starting point]'.
exercises.affirmation: You kept travaille in the present tense with depuis janvier.

summary.outcome: Translate English 'have been doing for/since' into French Present Tense + depuis.

use_example.german: Nous sommes amis depuis vingt ans.
use_example.english: We have been friends for twenty years.

summary.takeaway: Ongoing action = Present tense + depuis (for both 'for' and 'since').
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([2002] Since & For Gym): see how The Trap Lesson leads directly into Since & For Gym.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "My brother has been working here since January" in French:
twist.target_answer: Mon frère travaille ici depuis janvier
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Mon frère travaille ici depuis janvier" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of The Trap Lesson.

depuis.context_translation: I have lived here for three years (lit. I live here since three years).
depuis.etymology_derivation: Because the action is still true right now, French uses the PRESENT tense with depuis!

habiter.context_translation: I've lived here for three years.
habiter.etymology_derivation: habitāre 'to dwell often' — a habitat is where a thing dwells; habits are where you dwell repeatedly. With depuis, it stays present tense.

apprendre.etymology_derivation: An apprentice is literally 'one who is learning'.

attendre.context_translation: I am waiting for the train.
attendre.etymology_derivation: Latin attendere 'to stretch toward'. In French it means to wait for — with no preposition 'for' needed!

ans.context_translation: I'm thirty years old (I have thirty years).
ans.etymology_derivation: Latin annus — annual, anniversary. Age is something you have in French: j'ai X ans.

semaine.etymology_derivation: Latin septimāna, the seven-morning stretch. English had the same coin: sennight, seven nights — now extinct.

heure.etymology_derivation: Latin hōra. Silent H triggers elision: l'heure.

ion.name: The -ION Bridge
ion.phonetic_rule: Spelling converts 1:1; the final N is nasalised — thought, not said (collection /kɔlɛksjɔ̃/).
ion.historical_linguistics: English absorbed thousands of Latin-dress nouns through Norman French and later Renaissance borrowing. The -tion/-sion endings are the single largest cognate landing zone between the two languages.
ion.philological_note: Every -ION noun is feminine, so the article is la — elided to l' before a vowel. The ending is a gender decoder, not a memory item.
ion.literature_source: Walter, Le français dans tous les sens (1988); Pope, From Latin to Modern French (1952).

ation.name: The -ation Engine
ation.historical_linguistics: French -er verbs descend from Latin -āre; the English -ation nouns and French verbs are two leaves of the same Latin branch, so the noun unlocks the verb with almost no loss.
ation.philological_note: The whole -ation goes — célébration → célébrer, never *célébrater. Test for the -ation noun in English first; it is the proof the verb converts.
ation.literature_source: Guillaume, Temps et verbe (1929); standard French morphophonology.

ite.name: The -ité Bridge
ite.phonetic_rule: English final -ity becomes stressed final -ité /ite/ — the é marks the syllable English swallows.
ite.historical_linguistics: Latin -itās survives in English -ity and French -ité; both are bookish layers grafted onto the everyday vocabulary, which is why they convert with no sound loss.
ite.philological_note: All -ité nouns are feminine (la possibilité, la liberté).
ite.literature_source: Pope (1952); Brunot, Histoire de la langue française.

ance.name: The -ance/-ence Twins
ance.phonetic_rule: Same spelling family; the AN is nasal: différence /difeʁɑ̃s/.
ance.historical_linguistics: Latin -antia/-entia produced English -ance/-ence and French -ance/-ence directly; the pair is one of the highest-conversion zones in the vocabulary.

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).

ment.name: The -ment Adverb Bridge
ment.phonetic_rule: English -ly adverbs convert to -ment: exactement, rapidement — the ME is nasal, like pain.
ment.historical_linguistics: Latin -mente ('in a ... mind') became French -ment and English kept the same suffix for nouns (moment, comment) — but French built adverbs with it where English built them with -ly.
ment.philological_note: Feminine adjectives get an -e before -ment: exacte → exactement.

eur.name: The -eur Bridge
eur.phonetic_rule: Latin -or/-er nouns convert to -eur /œʁ/: doctor → docteur, color → couleur.
eur.historical_linguistics: The agent and quality suffixes of Latin split three ways in English (-or, -er, -our) but re-merge in French as -eur.
eur.philological_note: -eur is usually masculine — couleur and erreur are the famous rebels. The lesson names the exceptions before you trust the rule blindly.

able.name: The -able Bridge
able.phonetic_rule: Adjectives in -able/-ible convert as-is: adorable, possible, invisible — only the stress moves.
able.historical_linguistics: Latin -ābilis/-ibilis landed in both languages with the spelling intact; it is the highest-fidelity conversion family in the whole bridge.
able.philological_note: Same form, different stress: invisible with the beat on the final syllable in French.

doublet.name: Norman Doublets
doublet.phonetic_rule: Same Latin word entered English twice — once Germanic-dressed, once Norman: warden/gardien, estate/état, hôtel/hospital.
doublet.historical_linguistics: After 1066 English borrowed Norman French wholesale; centuries of independent drift mean many English words have a French twin that looks different and sounds different but is the same word.
doublet.philological_note: French dropped Latin H everywhere (hôtel, homme) and dropped S before consonants (état, école) — the dropped letters are the fingerprints.
